lessons.title: Count the work

outcomes.can: Count the steps a loop or a pair of nested loops takes for an input of size n.
Name the growth of a step count as constant, logarithmic, linear or quadratic.
Write a single pass and a nested pass over an array from a description.

lessons.intro: This course is about choosing how to store data and how to work on it, so that a program stays fast as its input grows. Every module explains an idea, shows it running, and then asks you to write code that is checked. This first module gives you the measuring tool that the rest of the course uses: counting the steps a piece of code takes, and describing how that count grows.

steps.title: Count steps, not seconds
steps.text:
The time a program takes depends on the machine, so seconds are a poor way to compare two solutions. A better measure is the number of basic steps the code performs, as a function of the size of its input. The size is usually called **n**: the length of an array, the number of items.

One loop over an array does about n steps. Two loops, one inside the other, do about n times n. What matters is how the count **grows** when n grows, because that decides whether the code still works on a large input.

steps.title: Predict the two counts
steps.text: Read the example. It counts the steps of a single loop and of a loop over every pair. Predict the output before you check.

steps.title: Read the counts
steps.text:
With 10 items the single loop took 10 steps and the pair loop 45. With 100 items they took 100 and 4,950.

Ten times the input made the single loop ten times the work. It made the pair loop about a hundred times the work. That difference is the whole subject of this course. At a million items the single loop takes a million steps, and the pair loop takes about five hundred billion.

steps.title: Name the growth
steps.text:
Growth is written with a capital O, which is read as "order of". Keep only the part that grows fastest and drop constant factors, because they do not change the shape.

| Name | Written | Steps for n = 1,000 | Typical code |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Constant | O(1) | 1 | Read one array element |
| Logarithmic | O(log n) | about 10 | Halve the range each time |
| Linear | O(n) | 1,000 | One loop |
| Linearithmic | O(n log n) | about 10,000 | A good sort |
| Quadratic | O(n²) | 1,000,000 | A loop inside a loop |

The pair loop took n(n - 1)/2 steps. Its fastest-growing part is n², so it is O(n²). The same measure applies to memory: an algorithm that builds a second array of the same length uses O(n) extra space.

steps.title: Why halving is so cheap
steps.text:
A million was cut to 1 in 19 steps. Doubling the input adds only one more step. That is logarithmic growth, and it is why searching sorted data, a later module, is so fast.

When you read code from now on, ask two questions. How many times does each loop run, in terms of n? And are the loops one after another, which adds their counts, or one inside another, which multiplies them?

lessons.title: Arrays and two pointers

outcomes.can: Say which array operations are constant and which move other elements.
Solve a problem in one pass with two indexes that move towards each other or side by side.
Combine two sorted arrays in one pass.

lessons.intro: An array is the structure you already use most. This module looks at what each array operation costs, which explains when an array is the right choice and when it is not. Then it introduces two pointers: a way to solve many array problems in one pass by moving two indexes.

steps.title: What an array is good at
steps.text:
An array keeps its elements side by side in memory, numbered from 0. Because of that, reading or writing the element at any index takes one step, however long the array is. So does adding or removing at the **end**.

The cost is at the front and in the middle. To insert at index 0, every existing element has to move one place along. To remove from the front, every later element moves back.

| Operation | Steps |
| --- | --- |
| Read or write `values[i]` | O(1) |
| `push` and `pop`, at the end | O(1) |
| `unshift` and `shift`, at the front | O(n) |
| Insert or remove in the middle, with `splice` | O(n) |
| Search for a value, with `indexOf` or `includes` | O(n) |

steps.title: Predict the cost at the front
steps.text: The example inserts at the front by hand, so that the moves can be counted. Predict what it prints.

steps.title: Every element moved
steps.text:
Inserting in front of 3 elements took 3 moves. In front of 1,000 it took 1,000. The built-in `unshift` does the same work out of sight.

This matters inside a loop. Calling `unshift` or `shift` n times costs about n² moves in total. Whenever you see one of them in a loop over a large array, look for a way to work at the end instead.

steps.title: Two pointers
steps.text:
Many array problems look as if they need a loop inside a loop, and can be done in one pass with two indexes. The indexes are called pointers.

- **Opposite ends.** One pointer starts at the front and one at the back, and they move towards each other. Use it to reverse, or to compare a sequence with its mirror image.
- **Side by side.** Both start at the front and move at their own pace, often one in each of two arrays. Use it to combine two sorted arrays.

Each pointer only ever moves forward, or only backward, so together they take at most n steps.

steps.title: Predict where the pointers stop

steps.title: They met in the middle
steps.text:
Each pass through the loop swapped one pair and moved both pointers inward. After two swaps both pointers were at index 2, the middle element, which needs no swap. The condition `left < right` stopped the loop there.

The array was changed **in place**: no second array was made, so the extra memory used is O(1). The condition matters. With `left <= right` the middle element would be swapped with itself, which is harmless. Looping over the whole length would swap every pair twice and undo the work.

lessons.title: Binary search

outcomes.can: Trace a binary search and say which elements it looks at.
Write a binary search that handles the first element, the last element and a missing value.
Find a boundary position, and search a range of numbers instead of an array.

lessons.intro: Looking for a value in an array normally means checking every element. When the array is sorted, there is a far faster way: look at the middle, and throw away the half that cannot hold the answer. This module covers binary search, the small mistakes that break it, and two variations that are used at least as often as the plain form.

steps.title: Halve the range
steps.text:
Binary search keeps a range of indexes, `low` to `high`, that could still hold the target. Each step looks at the element in the middle of that range.

- If it is the target, the search is over.
- If it is smaller than the target, the target can only be to the right, so `low` moves to one past the middle.
- If it is larger, `high` moves to one before the middle.

Each step halves the range, so a million elements need about 20 looks. This only works on **sorted** data. The comparison with the middle element says nothing about either half of an unsorted array.

steps.title: Predict what it looks at
steps.text: The example prints the range and the middle element at every step, then the result. Predict the output for a target of 23.

steps.title: Three looks among ten
steps.text:
The search looked at 16, then 56, then 23. Each look removed half of what was left: first indexes 0 to 4, then indexes 7 to 9.

Notice `low = middle + 1` and `high = middle - 1`. The middle element has just been checked, so it is left out of the new range. Keeping it in, with `low = middle`, is the classic mistake: when the range is two elements wide the middle is `low` itself, nothing changes, and the loop never ends.

steps.title: The parts that go wrong
steps.text:
Binary search is short and famously easy to get wrong. Three decisions must agree with each other.

- **What the range means.** Here `low` and `high` are both positions that could still hold the target.
- **When to stop.** With that meaning, a range of one element is still worth checking, so the loop runs while `low <= high`.
- **How to shrink.** Always leave out the middle that was just checked.

Test any binary search on four cases: the first element, the last element, a value that is missing, and an empty array. Most broken versions fail one of them.

steps.title: Predict a missing value
steps.text: The same search, counting its looks. Predict the output for a target that is not in the array.

steps.title: The range became empty
steps.text:
The search looked at 16, 5 and 2. After the third look `low` was 1 and `high` was 0. A range whose low end is past its high end is empty, so the loop ended and the function returned -1.

The value of `low` at that moment is useful: it is the position where the target would have to be inserted to keep the array sorted. The second exercise is built on that.

lessons.title: Maps and sets

outcomes.can: Use a Map to count or to look up, and a Set to remember what has been seen.
Replace a search inside a loop with a lookup, and say what it costs in memory.
Solve a pair problem in one pass by storing what you have already seen.

lessons.intro: Searching an array for a value takes a step for every element. A Map or a Set answers the same question in about one step, however much it holds. This module covers what those two structures do, why they are fast, and how they turn a loop inside a loop into a single pass.

steps.title: One step to find anything
steps.text:
A **Map** stores pairs of a key and a value. A **Set** stores keys only. Both answer "is this key here?" in about one step.

They manage it with **hashing**. A hash function turns a key into a number, and that number says where in an internal array the key is kept. To find a key, the structure computes the same number and looks in that one place. It never walks through the other keys.

| Operation | Map | Set | Steps |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Add or change | `map.set(key, value)` | `set.add(key)` | O(1) on average |
| Look up | `map.get(key)`, `map.has(key)` | `set.has(key)` | O(1) on average |
| Remove | `map.delete(key)` | `set.delete(key)` | O(1) on average |

The price is memory. A Set of n keys takes O(n) extra space. Trading memory for time in this way is one of the most common moves in programming.

steps.title: Predict a count
steps.text: The example counts how often each word appears. Predict both lines of output.

steps.title: Count with a Map
steps.text:
For each word, the loop read the count so far, used 0 when there was none, and stored one more. `counts.get("pink")` gave `undefined`, because that key was never set. The `??` operator supplies the 0 in that case.

The second line shows that a Map remembers the order in which keys were first added. The whole count took one pass over the words, with one lookup and one write for each.

steps.title: Replace a search with a lookup
steps.text:
Here is the pattern to recognize. A loop goes over the items, and for each item the code searches the rest of the list for something: a duplicate, a partner, a match. That inner search makes the whole thing O(n²).

Keep a Set or a Map of what has been seen so far. The inner search becomes one lookup, and the whole thing becomes O(n).

Keys are compared the way `===` compares them. Numbers and strings work as you expect. Two different arrays or objects are different keys even when their contents are equal, so build a string key when you need to look up by contents.

steps.title: Remember what was seen
steps.text:
The loop looked at 4, 9 and 2, adding each to the set. The fourth value, 9, was already there, so the function returned at once after four lookups. It never reached the second 4.

With an array in place of the set, each check would have searched everything seen so far. For a long list with no repeats, that is the difference between n lookups and about n²/2 comparisons.

lessons.title: Stacks and queues

outcomes.can: Predict the order in which a stack and a queue give items back.

lessons.intro: Some problems only ever need the newest item, and some only the oldest. A stack and a queue are arrays used with that one restriction. The restriction is the point: it makes the code simpler, and it makes every operation take one step. This module covers both, and the trap in building a queue on an array.

steps.title: Last in, first out
steps.text:
A **stack** gives back the item that was added most recently. Think of a pile of plates: you add to the top and take from the top. The two operations are **push**, which adds, and **pop**, which removes and returns the newest.

An array is a ready-made stack. `push` and `pop` both work at the end, so each takes one step.

A stack fits any problem where the thing you need next is the most recent thing you have not dealt with yet: matching brackets, undo, working out an expression, and following a path that you may need to back out of.

steps.text:
Three letters went on: a, b, c. The two pops returned c and then b, the newest first. Then d was pushed on top of a, so the stack held a and d.

`pop` on an empty array returns `undefined` and does not fail. Code that uses a stack usually has to decide what an empty stack means: in the bracket exercise below it means a closing bracket with nothing to match.

steps.title: First in, first out
steps.text:
A **queue** gives back the item that has waited longest, like a line of people. The operations are **enqueue**, which adds at the back, and **dequeue**, which removes from the front.

An array can add at the back in one step with `push`. Removing from the front with `shift` is the trap: as the module on arrays showed, `shift` moves every remaining element, so it costs O(n). A queue that is emptied with `shift` costs O(n²) in total.

The fix is not to remove anything. Keep an index, `head`, that marks where the front of the queue is, and move the index forward. Reading the front and moving the index are both one step.

The array itself still holds a and b. They are simply behind the head and never looked at again. The number of items waiting is the array's length minus `head`. The later module on graphs uses exactly this queue.

lessons.title: Linked lists

outcomes.can: Walk a linked list from its head and say what each step costs.
Insert and remove nodes by changing links in the right order.
Reverse a linked list without losing the rest of it.

lessons.intro: An array keeps its elements side by side, which is why inserting at the front is slow. A linked list makes the opposite trade. Each element sits in its own small object, called a node, with a link to the next one. This module covers walking a list, changing its links, and the two mistakes that lose part of a list.

steps.title: Nodes and links
steps.text:
A **linked list** is a chain of nodes. Each node holds a value and a link, `next`, to the node after it. The last node's `next` is `null`. The list as a whole is known by its first node, the **head**.

There are no indexes. To reach the fifth node you start at the head and follow four links. So reading by position costs O(n), where an array costs O(1).

What a list gains is at the links. If you already hold a node, inserting or removing right after it means changing one or two links, and nothing else moves.

| Operation | Array | Linked list |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Read the element at a position | O(1) | O(n) |
| Insert or remove at the front | O(n) | O(1) |
| Insert or remove after a node you hold | O(n) | O(1) |
| Search for a value | O(n) | O(n) |

steps.title: Predict a walk

steps.title: One hop for each node
steps.text:
The loop started at the head, printed its value, and followed `next` until it reached `null`. It printed 10, 20 and 30, and took three hops.

This loop is the basic shape of nearly all list code: `for (let node = head; node !== null; node = node.next)`. The variable has the type `ListNode | null`, and the condition is what tells TypeScript that `node` is a real node inside the loop.

steps.title: Change links in the right order
steps.text:
To insert a node b between a and c, two links change: b must point to c, and a must point to b.

The order matters. `a.next` is the only way to reach c. If you set `a.next = b` first, the link to c is gone, and everything after it is lost. So first copy the old link into the new node, and only then redirect the old node.

The rule in general: **before you overwrite a link, make sure something else still points to what it pointed to.**

The new node b was created with its `next` already set to `a.next`, which was c. Then `a.next` was pointed at b. The chain is now a, b, c, and c is still the last node, so its `next` is `null`.

Removing is the reverse. To remove the node after a, set `a.next = a.next.next`. The removed node is no longer reachable from the list.

lessons.title: Recursion

outcomes.can: Trace the calls a recursive function makes, going in and coming back.
Count the calls a recursive function makes and say how they grow.
Write a recursive function with a base case and a smaller call.

lessons.intro: Some problems contain smaller copies of themselves: a folder holds folders, a list is one item followed by a shorter list. A recursive function solves such a problem by calling itself on the smaller copy. This module covers how to write one, what the computer does while it runs, and how recursion can be very fast or very slow.

steps.title: Two parts of a recursive function
steps.text:
A **recursive** function calls itself. To finish, it needs two parts.

- A **base case**: an input so small that the answer is known at once, with no further call.
- A **recursive case**: the function calls itself on a **smaller** input and uses the result.

Every call must move towards the base case. A function with no base case, or one whose calls do not get smaller, never stops. In practice it stops with the error "Maximum call stack size exceeded".

The useful way to write one is to trust it. Assume the call on the smaller input already returns the right answer, and ask only: how do I get my answer from that?

steps.title: Predict the order
steps.text: The function prints before and after it calls itself. Predict the five lines.

steps.title: Going in and coming back
steps.text:
The calls went in: `countdown(2)` printed 2 and called `countdown(1)`, which printed 1 and called `countdown(0)`, which printed done and returned.

Then they came back out in reverse. `countdown(1)` continued after its call and printed back 1. Then `countdown(2)` continued and printed back 2.

While a call waits for the call inside it, the computer keeps its variables on the **call stack**. That is a stack in the sense of the earlier module: the most recent call finishes first. A recursion n calls deep uses O(n) memory for that stack, even when the code creates nothing else.

steps.title: How many calls?
steps.text:
The cost of a recursive function is the number of calls it makes, times the work in each.

- A function that makes **one** call on an input one smaller makes n calls. That is a loop written another way.
- A function that makes one call on an input **half** the size makes about log n calls. Binary search is the example.
- A function that makes **two** calls on inputs one smaller can make about 2ⁿ calls. Each level of calls doubles the one before.

So the shape of the calls decides everything. Draw them as a tree when you are unsure: one branch for each call.

steps.title: Ten more, a hundred times the work

For 10 the function was called 177 times. For 20 it was called 21,891 times. Adding 10 to the input multiplied the work by more than a hundred.

The reason is repeated work. `fib(20)` calls `fib(19)` and `fib(18)`. But `fib(19)` also calls `fib(18)`, which is worked out all over again, and so on all the way down. The module on dynamic programming removes that repetition.

lessons.title: Sorting

outcomes.can: Trace insertion sort and say why it takes about n² steps.

lessons.intro: Sorted data is what makes binary search, merging and many other fast techniques possible, so sorting is worth understanding from the inside. This module covers one simple sort, one fast sort, and how to use the built-in sort correctly, which is what you will do in practice.

steps.title: A simple sort
steps.text:
**Insertion sort** works the way most people sort a hand of cards. Keep the left part of the array sorted. Take the next element, and slide it left past every element that is larger, until it is in place.

Each element may have to slide past all the elements before it. In the worst case, an array in reverse order, that is 1 + 2 + ... + (n - 1) moves, which is about n²/2. So insertion sort is O(n²).

It has two real merits. On an array that is already nearly sorted it does almost no work, close to O(n). And it needs no extra memory.

steps.title: Predict each pass
steps.text: The example prints the array after each element is put in place. Predict the three lines.

steps.title: One element at a time
steps.text:
First 2 slid in front of 5. Then 4 slid in front of 5 and stopped behind 2. Last, 1 slid past all three.

The inner loop shifts larger elements one place to the right to make a gap, and the saved element is written into the gap. Its condition has two parts, and both matter: `j >= 0` stops at the front of the array, and `values[j] > current` stops at the first element that is not larger.

steps.title: A fast sort
steps.text:
**Merge sort** is recursive. Split the array into two halves, sort each half with the same function, and then **merge** the two sorted halves. Merging is the two-pointer pass from the module on arrays, and it takes n steps.

The base case is an array of one element or none, which is already sorted.

Count the work by levels. The array is halved until the pieces have one element, which takes log n levels. At every level, all the merging together handles n elements. So the total is n times log n, written **O(n log n)**. For a million elements that is about 20 million steps, where insertion sort needs about 500 billion.

Merge sort uses O(n) extra memory for the merged halves.

steps.title: Predict the built-in sort
steps.text: In practice you call the built-in sort. Predict all three lines. The second line has a surprise.

steps.title: Comparators and stability
steps.text:
With no argument, `sort` compares elements **as text**. As text, "10" comes before "9", because "1" comes before "9". That gave 1, 10, 100, 9.

A **comparator** fixes it. It is a function of two elements that returns a negative number when the first should come first, a positive number when the second should, and 0 when they are equal in order. `(a, b) => a - b` sorts numbers from smallest to largest.

The first line shows **stability**. Two tasks with the same priority kept the order they had before: call before mail, and write before plan. The built-in sort is stable, and so is a merge sort that takes from the left half on a tie. Stability is what lets you sort by one field and then by another.

Note also that `sort` changes the array it is called on. Copy first, with `[...values]`, when the caller's array must stay as it was.

lessons.intro: A linked list gives each node one link. Give each node two, and the chain becomes a tree: a structure that branches. Trees appear wherever things contain other things, and a tree kept in order can be searched as fast as a sorted array while still allowing cheap inserts. This module covers walking a binary tree and searching a binary search tree.

steps.title: Nodes with two links
steps.text:
A **binary tree** is made of nodes. Each node holds a value and two links, `left` and `right`, each to another node or to `null`. The node at the top is the **root**. A node with no children is a **leaf**.

Every node is itself the root of a smaller tree, called a **subtree**. That is why recursion fits trees so well: do something with the node, and ask the same function about its left and right subtrees. The base case is an empty tree, `null`.

The **height** of a tree is the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down to a leaf. A tree of n nodes has a height of about log n when it is bushy, and of n when every node has only one child, which is a linked list in disguise.

steps.title: Predict a walk

steps.title: Left, node, right
steps.text:
The walk went as far left as it could before printing anything, so 1 came first. It printed 3 only after everything to the left of 3, and 8 only after the whole left subtree.

This order is called **in-order**. There are two others, which differ only in where the node itself is handled: **pre-order** handles the node before its subtrees, and **post-order** after both. Whichever order is used, every node is visited once, so a full walk costs O(n).

steps.title: A tree kept in order
steps.text:
A **binary search tree** adds one rule. For every node, all the values in its left subtree are smaller than the node's value, and all the values in its right subtree are larger.

The rule makes searching fast. Compare the target with the root. If the target is smaller, it can only be in the left subtree, so the whole right subtree is ignored. This is binary search, laid out as a structure.

A search follows one path from the root, so it costs as many steps as the tree is high: O(log n) for a bushy tree. The rule has another consequence. An in-order walk of a binary search tree visits the values from smallest to largest.

outcomes.can: Find the parent and the children of a position in a heap stored in an array.

lessons.intro: Often you do not need everything in order. You only need the smallest item, again and again: the next job to run, the nearest place to visit. A heap is built for exactly that. It gives the smallest item at once and takes about log n steps to add or remove one. This module covers how a heap is laid out in a plain array and the two operations that keep it valid.

steps.title: A tree packed into an array
steps.text:
A **min-heap** is a binary tree with one rule: every node's value is less than or equal to the values of its children. So the smallest value is always at the root. Nothing is promised about left against right, and a heap is **not** fully sorted.

A heap is always filled level by level, from left to right, with no gaps. That lets it live in an array with no links at all. The root is at index 0, and positions are found by arithmetic.

| For the node at index i | Index |
| --- | --- |
| Its parent | `Math.floor((i - 1) / 2)` |
| Its left child | `2 * i + 1` |
| Its right child | `2 * i + 2` |

Because the tree has no gaps, its height is about log n. Every heap operation walks one path between the root and a leaf, which is why they cost O(log n).

Notice that the array is not sorted: 3 comes before 2. A heap keeps just enough order to know where the smallest is.

steps.title: Sift up and sift down
steps.text:
**To add a value**, put it at the end of the array, which is the next free place in the bottom level. It may now be smaller than its parent. While it is, swap the two and continue from the parent's position. This is called **sifting up**.

**To remove the smallest**, take the root. To fill the hole, move the last element of the array to the root. It is probably too large for that place. While it is larger than its smaller child, swap it with that child and continue from there. This is **sifting down**.

Always swap with the **smaller** child when sifting down. The smaller child is about to become the parent of the other one, so it has to be the smaller of the two.

Seven elements needed at most two swaps. A heap of a million elements needs at most twenty. Only the nodes on one path from a leaf to the root were touched.

outcomes.can: Store a graph as a list of neighbours for each node.

lessons.intro: A tree is a special case of something more general. Places joined by roads, people who know each other, tasks that depend on other tasks: each is a set of things with connections between them, called a graph. This module covers how to store a graph and how to explore it level by level, which finds the route with the fewest steps.

steps.title: Nodes and edges
steps.text:
A **graph** has **nodes**, which are the things, and **edges**, which are the connections between pairs of them. An edge can be two-way, as with a road, or one-way, as with "must be done before". A graph with one-way edges is called **directed**.

Unlike a tree, a graph has no root, and it may contain **cycles**: you can leave a node and come back to it by another route.

The usual way to store a graph is an **adjacency list**: for each node, the list of its neighbours. In this course that is an object from a name to an array of names. A two-way edge between a and b appears twice, once in each list.

steps.title: Predict the size

steps.title: Each road is listed twice
steps.text:
There are 5 places. Adding up the lengths of all the neighbour lists gives 10, and every two-way road was counted from both of its ends, so there are 5 roads.

Any algorithm that looks at every node and every neighbour list once costs O(n + e), for n nodes and e edges. That is the cost of every graph algorithm in this course.

steps.title: Breadth-first search
steps.text:
**Breadth-first search** explores a graph in rings. First the starting node, then all its neighbours, then all of their neighbours that are new, and so on.

It needs two things. A **queue** holds the nodes that have been found and not yet explored, oldest first. A **set of seen nodes** makes sure each node is added to the queue only once.

The seen set is not optional. A graph can have cycles, and without the set the search would walk round a cycle for ever. Mark a node as seen at the moment it is **added** to the queue, not when it is taken out, or it can be added several times.

Because nodes are explored in order of distance, the first time breadth-first search reaches a node is by a route with the fewest edges.

The queue is the array itself, read with a `head` index as in the module on queues. Nothing is ever removed, so at the end the array holds every reached node in the order it was found.

lessons.title: Depth-first search and ordering

outcomes.can: Explore a graph depth first and predict when each node is entered and left.

lessons.intro: Breadth-first search explores in rings. The other way to explore is to follow one route as far as it goes, and only then back up and try another. That is depth-first search. It is short to write with recursion, and it answers questions that rings cannot: whether a graph has a cycle, and in what order to do things that depend on each other.

steps.title: Go deep, then back up
steps.text:
**Depth-first search** starts at a node and moves to a neighbour it has not seen, then to a neighbour of that one, and so on. When a node has no unseen neighbours left, the search **backs up** to the node it came from and continues with that node's next neighbour.

Recursion does the backing up for you. A function `visit(node)` marks the node as seen and calls itself on each unseen neighbour. When a call returns, the search is back at the node before.

It visits every node and edge once, so it costs O(n + e), the same as breadth-first search. The differences are the order and what it finds. Depth-first search does **not** find the route with the fewest steps. Like breadth-first search, it needs a seen set, or a cycle makes it recurse for ever.

The search entered a, then b, then d. Node d has no neighbours, so it was left at once. Then b was left. Back at a, the search entered c. From c the neighbour d was already seen, so c was left, and last of all a.

Look at the leave order: d, b, c, a. A node is left only after everything reachable from it has been left. That one fact is the basis of both ideas in the rest of this module.

steps.title: Cycles and order
steps.text:
**Finding a cycle.** In a directed graph, a cycle exists when the search, while exploring from some node, arrives back at a node that is **still being explored**: one that has been entered and not yet left. Such a node is on the current path, so there is a route from it back to itself.

Arriving at a node that was entered **and left** earlier is not a cycle. It only means two routes lead to the same place. So one seen set is not enough. Track three states for each node: not visited, being visited, and done.

**Ordering by need.** Suppose an edge from x to y means "x needs y first". Then the leave order is a valid order to do things in: a node is left only after everything it needs has been left. An order in which every item comes after what it needs is called a **topological order**. It exists only when the graph has no cycle.

lessons.intro: The module on recursion ended with a function that took 21,891 calls to work out one small number, because it kept solving the same smaller problems again. Dynamic programming is the fix: solve each smaller problem once, and remember its answer. This module covers the two ways to do that, and how to recognize a problem it applies to.

steps.title: Remember the answers
steps.text:
Some recursive functions call themselves with the same input many times. When that happens, the smaller problems **overlap**, and most of the work is repetition.

**Memoization** removes it. Keep a Map from an input to its answer. At the start of each call, look the input up. If the answer is there, return it. If not, work it out as before, and store it before returning.

The function is otherwise unchanged, and each distinct input is now worked out once. The cost becomes the number of distinct inputs times the work for one of them.

steps.text: This is the function from the module on recursion, with a memo added. It took 21,891 calls there. Predict both lines.

steps.title: From 21,891 calls to 39
steps.text:
The answer is the same, 6765, and it took 39 calls. Each value from 2 to 20 was worked out once. Its second request was answered from the Map.

The second line asks for the fiftieth number. Without the memo that would take tens of billions of calls. With it, the answer appears at once. The cost went from about 2ⁿ to about n, in exchange for O(n) memory.

steps.title: Fill a table from the bottom
steps.text:
Memoization starts at the big problem and works down. The other way is to start at the smallest problems and work **up**, storing each answer in an array. This is called **tabulation**, and it needs no recursion at all.

To design either kind, answer three questions.

1. **What does one entry mean?** For example: entry i is the number of ways to climb i steps.
2. **How does an entry follow from earlier ones?** For example: the last move was one step or two, so entry i is entry i - 1 plus entry i - 2.
3. **Which entries are known at the start?** For example: there is one way to climb 0 steps, and one way to climb 1.

Once those are written down, the code is a loop. Most of the difficulty in dynamic programming is in the first question.

steps.title: Predict a table
steps.text: The table holds the number of ways to climb a staircase, taking one or two steps at a time. Predict the line it prints.

steps.title: Each entry from the two before
steps.text:
The table started with 1 and 1. Each later entry is the sum of the two entries before it: 2, 3, 5, 8, 13. So there are 13 ways to climb six steps.

Only the last two entries are ever read. When that is true, the table can be replaced by two variables, and the memory drops from O(n) to O(1).

lessons.title: Choose the structure

outcomes.can: Pick a data structure by the operation a problem repeats most often.
Recognize when sorting first makes a problem a single pass.
Model a new problem as a graph and choose the search that fits.

lessons.intro: This last module has no new structures. Real problems do not say which structure to use, so the skill that remains is choosing. The module gives a short way to decide, shows how much the choice can matter, and then sets three problems with no hint about which earlier module they belong to.

steps.title: Ask what is repeated
steps.text:
To choose a structure, find the operation the solution performs again and again, and pick the structure that makes that one operation cheap.

| The repeated operation | Structure | Cost of it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Read by position | Array | O(1) |
| Is this value present? Look up by key | Set or Map | O(1) on average |
| Take the most recent | Stack | O(1) |
| Take the oldest | Queue | O(1) |
| Take the smallest | Heap | O(log n) |
| Find a position in ordered data | Sorted array with binary search | O(log n) |
| Insert or remove next to a known place | Linked list | O(1) |

Then ask the same of the algorithm. Does the problem have the shape of a walk through connected things, of a choice built from smaller choices, or of a single pass that only needs the data in order?

steps.title: Predict the difference
steps.text: Both halves of the example answer one question: does any number in a also appear in b? Predict the two step counts.

steps.title: The same answer, 500 times cheaper
steps.text:
The nested loops compared every pair: a million steps. The second version spent 1,000 steps building a Set from b and 1,000 lookups, 2,000 in all.

Nothing about the problem changed. The repeated operation was "is this value in b?", and a Set answers that in one step where an array needs a scan. Most speed-ups in everyday code are this one.

steps.title: Sort first
steps.text:
A second move is worth as much as the first: **put the data in order before working on it**. Sorting costs O(n log n), and it often turns the rest of the problem into one pass.

- After sorting, equal items are next to each other, so duplicates and groups are found by comparing neighbours.
- After sorting by start time, things that overlap are next to each other.
- After sorting, binary search and two pointers both become available.

When a problem seems to need every pair compared, ask whether an order exists in which only neighbours matter.

steps.title: Predict a sweep
steps.text: The example sorts meetings by start time and then compares each with the one before it. Predict both lines.

steps.title: Only neighbours were compared
steps.text:
After sorting, the meetings read 9 to 10, 9 to 11, 13 to 15 and 14 to 16. The loop found that the second starts before the first ends, and that the fourth starts before the third ends: two overlaps.

Unsorted, finding those would mean comparing every meeting with every other. Sorted, three comparisons were enough. The first exercise extends this to merging the overlapping ranges.

tasks.title: Find the shortest way through a grid
tasks.prompt: grid is a list of rows of equal length. In each row "." is an open cell and "#" is a wall. Return the fewest moves needed to get from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell, moving one cell up, down, left or right at a time, through open cells only. hints: This is a graph. What are its nodes, and which nodes are connected?
Each open cell is a node, connected to the open cells next to it. The fewest moves in such a graph is found by breadth-first search.
Keep the number of moves for each cell, with -1 for not reached. Start a queue with [0, 0]. For each cell, try the four neighbours that are inside the grid, open and not yet reached.
